# SwiftParcel ETA serving — Assignment 5

**Roll number:** DA24B003  
**Machine:** Ubuntu Linux ARM64 VM on a Mac; 4 CPU cores, 3.3 GiB RAM, Python 3.11.18; CPU only.  
**Reproduction:** See `README.md`. Data and model bundles are generated by the supplied `eta_data.py`; model files and the SQLite database are excluded from the ZIP.

## Part A — REST service

`eta_app.py` loads the selected bundle once, validates seven features and the infeasible combination, returns rounded predictions with request IDs, and exposes `/healthz` and Prometheus `/metrics`. The TestClient suite passed **21 cases**. The one-worker v1 server was measured for four seconds at each concurrency with batch size 1 and no access log.

| Clients | Requests/s | p50 ms | p95 ms | p99 ms | Errors |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 486.5 | 2.0 | 2.4 | 3.2 | 0 |
| 2 | 675.0 | 2.9 | 3.2 | 4.1 | 0 |
| 4 | 561.2 | 6.2 | 11.9 | 22.5 | 0 |
| 8 | 617.8 | 12.1 | 20.8 | 29.4 | 0 |
| 16 | 603.8 | 25.2 | 42.0 | 63.3 | 0 |

Throughput peaked at two clients and then stayed near 600 requests/s while latency rose, so the server was saturated by about 2–4 clients. Little's Law for this closed-loop test gives mean in-system time near `L/λ = 16/603.8 = 26.5 ms` at 16 clients, consistent with the 25.2 ms median. The highest **observed** throughput meeting p95 ≤80 ms was 675.0 requests/s; every tested load met the SLO, and loads beyond 16 clients were not measured.

At concurrency 1, batch 1 achieved 473.2 requests/s and 2.1133 ms/row; batch 100 achieved 337.8 requests/s and 0.0296 ms/row, with no errors. These values use `1000/(requests/s × rows/request)`. Batching amortizes HTTP and Python overhead and lets the model process rows together.

I proposed two Uvicorn workers to use more of the VM's four cores and reran the same load test. At concurrency 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, throughput was 462.2, 724.5, 882.0, 1053.0, and 1149.8 requests/s; p95 was 2.8, 4.1, 7.7, 12.3, and 22.4 ms, with zero errors. The best measured SLO-compliant throughput improved **1.70×** (675.0 → 1149.8 requests/s), short of doubling. The counter and histogram in this simple app are process-local, so production deployment with multiple workers would need shared metric aggregation.

p95 and p99 show the slow requests that users notice and that can breach an SLO. A mean can stay low while queueing or occasional stalls make those tail requests much slower.

## Part B — MLflow registry, gate, and shadow

The custom pyfunc returns a DataFrame with one-decimal `eta_minutes` and `model_version`. Both models were logged with an input example, inferred input/output signature, and exact package-version requirements, then registered in a SQLite-backed `eta-model` registry.

| Registry version | Bundle | Alias |
|---:|---|---|
| 1 | v1 Ridge | `prod` |
| 2 | v2 GradientBoostingRegressor | `candidate` |

The pure `decide()` function passed **8 boundary-aware tests**. `promotion_gate()` evaluated 2,000 fresh rows generated with seed 99 and timed 200 single-row predictions per alias. At default thresholds, prod/candidate MAE was **11.9553/6.10485 min**, rush MAE **19.6799/8.5795**, rain MAE **11.6227/6.2853**, and p95 **1.701/1.512 ms**; all criteria passed, so `promote=true`. With `min_rel_gain=0.60`, the measured MAE gain of **48.9%** failed that criterion, so `promote=false`; the other criteria passed. Full outputs are in `partB/gate_output.txt`.

Two local MLflow servers received the same 200 one-row fresh requests on ports 5101 (prod) and 5102 (candidate), with a mean absolute prediction difference of 9.484 min, 35.0% differing by more than 10 min, and server p95 latencies of 4.956 ms and 5.369 ms, respectively. I would promote v2 into a guarded 10% canary because it substantially improves fresh-data and slice MAE and meets the latency gate, while the prediction differences warrant monitoring. Moving an alias does not change a running server because it resolved and loaded its model at startup. A rolling restart behind a health-checked load balancer lets new instances load the new alias target while old instances finish their requests. Alternatively, the service can load the new model beside the old one and atomically switch a version-aware handle after readiness checks, allowing in-flight requests to finish and a quick rollback.

## Part C — Ray Serve sticky canary

`build()` binds two v1 replicas, an autoscaled v2 deployment (min 1, max 3), and a FastAPI router. Each replica reserves 0.25 CPU, so even the maximum six replicas including the router reserve only **1.5 of 2 Ray CPUs**. SHA-256 maps each customer ID to a stable bucket; increasing the weight only adds customers to v2.

On a fresh two-CPU Ray run, **213/1000 (21.3%)** distinct customers went to v2 at weight 0.2, within the required ±4 percentage points. All 200 repeated calls and all 200 calls after an identical redeploy kept their arm. At weight 0.5, v2 share was 50.9% and **zero** prior v2 customers moved back; `X-Beta: 1` forced v2 for 50/50 selected prod customers. All five assertions passed in `partC/verify_output.txt`.

Python's built-in `hash()` is salted per process, so its buckets can change after restart or across replicas. Stickiness keeps a customer's ETA behavior consistent and avoids treatment switching that would contaminate the experiment's comparison. The candidate keeps one warm replica to avoid cold starts and scales toward two ongoing requests per replica. A five-second upscale delay responds to sustained load, while a 30-second downscale delay avoids rapid oscillation. The three-replica cap and fractional CPU reservations fit the two-CPU test cluster.

## Part D — release gate

The smoke script checks health/version, valid and rounded output, two model-sanity rules, batch order, invalid-input 422, request-ID echo, and 30-request p95. Against v1 it passed all checks with **p95 9.52 ms ≤80 ms** and exit code **0**. A wrong expected version must exit **1**.

| Abort a 10% v2 canary if… | Threshold and window |
|---|---|
| Server errors | v2 HTTP 5xx rate >1% over a rolling 5 minutes, with ≥100 v2 requests |
| Tail latency | v2 prediction p95 >80 ms over a rolling 5 minutes, with ≥100 v2 requests |
| Realized ETA quality | v2 MAE >v1 shadow MAE by >5% over a rolling 24 hours, with ≥100 completed deliveries per arm |
| Routing balance | v2 receives <6% or >14% of newly seen customer IDs over a rolling 15 minutes, with ≥1,000 distinct IDs |

**Not tested:** real production traffic and delivery labels, multi-node Ray, and a live rolling restart/hot swap. All reported numeric results above came from the local VM runs. Course concepts were reviewed from the [REST serving](https://github.com/sudarsun/DA3408/blob/main/Lecture%2010%20--%20REST_API_Serving_Exercise.ipynb), [MLflow serving](https://github.com/sudarsun/DA3408/blob/main/Lecture%2010%20--%20MLflow_Serving_Exercise.ipynb), and [Ray Serve](https://github.com/sudarsun/DA3408/blob/main/Lecture%2010%20--%20Ray_Serve_Exercise.ipynb) lecture notebooks; the SwiftParcel implementation was written for this assignment.
